structured_output.summary:
I found no public CIFAR-100 submission faster than the loop's own tip. The official AIDDA/Daniel-T-S-Adams benchmark repo has an empty submissions/ folder, no PRs and one fresh fork. Its verified baseline is a ResNet9 at 75.36% in 59.3 s. The only public CIFAR-100 recipe found is futurebiohackers PR #3 (75.29% in 8.11 s), which the loop already beat.

The most actionable new evidence comes from three places:
(1) Fable e1 and hiverge train the whitening bias for only 0.2 epochs, not 20% of steps. Fable keys its compiled full-step graphs on (resolution, whiten_bias_grad), so it switches requires_grad off rather than setting LR to 0. E061 used the LR route, which cannot skip any compute, so H2.15.1 is still untested as a FLOP lever.
(2) MaxSup, a zero-cost replacement for label smoothing, beat LS by 0.77 pp on CIFAR-100 ResNet-18 and 0.27 pp on ResNet-50. It is a new candidate for H6.
(3) The spectral feature-learning condition predicts that the 576->100 Muon head's update scale should be sqrt(100/576) ≈ 0.42x of the hidden-layer scale. This gives a principled reason for the head lr 0.5x gain (H7.3.2) and suggests ~0.4x as the next point.

On H2.16 (fused BN/GELU), PyTorch only gained fused normalization-backward codegen (MixOrderReduction, split-size autotuning) in 2.11, aimed at H100/B200. In torch 2.4, BN backward likely still reads dy twice (once for the per-channel reductions, once for dX). A hand-written Triton kernel is the only route, which is consistent with the E066 null.

EfficientNetV2 found that scaling regularization with image size adds +0.7-0.8 pp over plain progressive resizing. That suggests a phase-dependent label smoothing (lower LS at 16/24 px). It is low-to-moderate prior here because E037 (a uniform LS change) was null.

Fable and hiverge also freeze the BN weight (bias-only BN, eps 1e-12). The loop should check whether the tip already does this; if not, it is a small dW-reduction saving.

No new evidence was found for momentum schedules (critical damping is weak on CIFAR-100), randomized polar decomposition (no numbers) or Muon variants on CNNs.

findings.claim: hiverge trains the whitening bias only while step < 0.2*len(train_loader), i.e. about 0.2 epoch, not 20% of total steps (`whiten_bias_grad = step < whiten_bias_train_steps`). BN is defined with weight.requires_grad=False (bias-only BN), momentum 1-0.5566 and eps 1e-12. The head is bias-free, its logits are divided by x.size(-1), and it is on SGD at lr 0.5415 with weight_decay=wd/head_lr, where wd = 1.0418e-6*batch_size. The LR decays linearly to 0.
findings.relevance: E061 froze the bias after 20% of steps (1.6 epochs), about 8x later than the public recipes. It did so through an LR mask, so no backward compute was removed. A requires_grad=False freeze at ~0.2 epoch is the version that actually removes FLOPs. The code also confirms H7.3.3's head wd setting, but only for an SGD head. Bias-only BN is worth checking on the tip, since freezing the BN weight saves one per-channel reduction per BN in backward.

findings.claim: Fable e1 sets whiten_bias_epochs: 0.2 and captures a FullStepGraph per (resolution, whiten_bias_grad) key, so the frozen-bias steps run a different graph. It also uses bias-only BN (weight frozen, eps 1e-12), SiLU, label smoothing 0.09, brightness/contrast jitter, the GlobalAmaxPool via flatten(2).max(dim=2).values, bs 1536, a 24/28/32 res schedule, and a final EMA every 4 steps (decay 0.7) starting 8 steps before the decay ends, with an LR floor of 0.05.
findings.relevance: This confirms that the public record implements the bias freeze as a separate compiled graph with the bias grad off. That design only pays off if the grad is skipped (no dgrad into the stem output). It directly supports the H2.15.1 design (static graphs keyed by bias-grad) and suggests a much earlier freeze point (0.2 epoch, ~6-7 steps at 16 px for CIFAR-100 at bs 1536 would be 0.2*33 steps).

findings.claim: MaxSup replaces label smoothing with the penalty L = α(z_max − mean_k z_k), which penalizes the top-1 logit rather than the ground-truth logit, added to plain CE. CIFAR-100 ResNet-18: baseline 76.16, LS 77.05, MaxSup 77.82 (+0.77 pp over LS). ResNet-50: 78.69 / 78.88 / 79.15. ImageNet ResNet-50: 76.41 / 76.91 / 77.69.
findings.relevance: This is a new zero-time-cost accuracy lever for H6, which needs +0.1-0.3 pp to fund cuts. It is a one-line loss change: compute max and mean over the 100 logits, which is negligible next to the head. The evidence comes from long (200-epoch) schedules, and the run uses LS 0.3, which is much heavier than in the paper. Matching α to the LS strength, e.g. α≈0.3, and two-run scoring are needed. Prior is moderate-low, but it is untested and orthogonal to the closed LS-value knob (E009, E037).

findings.claim: EfficientNetV2 progressive learning scales regularization (dropout, RandAugment magnitude, mixup) up with image size. Its Table 13 ablation gives progressive resize 84.3±0.14 vanilla vs 85.1±0.07 with adaptive regularization (+0.8 pp), and random resize 83.5 vs 84.2 (+0.7 pp).
findings.relevance: This suggests a zero-cost, phase-dependent regularization schedule: weaker label smoothing (e.g. 0.1-0.15) in the 16/24 px phases and 0.3 in the 32 px tail. Under the loop's evidence, more regularization hurts under-fitted short runs (E008), while a uniform LS change was null (E037). A per-phase LS is therefore a distinct and untested variant. Prior is low-moderate. It is cheap to implement as a 0-d tensor LS or a per-phase loss.

findings.claim: The spectral condition for feature learning says that weight matrices and their updates should have spectral norm scaling like sqrt(fan_out/fan_in).
findings.relevance: The tip's head (576->100) uses the Muon scale sqrt(max(1, out/in)) = 1. The spectral condition instead gives sqrt(100/576) ≈ 0.42. This is a principled explanation of why head lr 0.5x helped (E049/E062/E063 pool +~0.15 pp) and suggests 0.4x as the next point to test. It is a zero-cost 0-d tensor change. A further step to ~0.3x would bracket the optimum.

findings.claim: Inductor's fused normalization-backward codegen (MixOrderReduction: the inner dX reduction and the outer dW/dB reduction fused in one pass with split-reduction workspaces, plus num_stages autotuning) was introduced around torch 2.11. It gave ~2x over previous torch.compile on LayerNorm backward and up to 20% from software pipelining. The poor split-size choice of older inductor caused >2x degradation. Non-power-of-2 widths such as N=384 show small regressions in Triton.
findings.relevance: For channels_last BN (rows = N*H*W, cols = C), torch 2.4 likely emits the per-channel reductions and the dX pointwise as separate passes over dy and x. A hand-written fused BN+GELU backward in Triton would remove one full read of dy and x per layer. That is the only route left after E066 (inductor tuning flags null), and it explains why. The note on width 384 fits the E050/H2.13.2 tile-misalignment question. Effort is high; the expected gain is bounded by about 30% elementwise × fraction of redundant passes.

findings.claim: In-Place Activated BatchNorm fuses BN and activation into one layer and recomputes the BN input from the stored output by inverting the activation. It saves up to 50% of training memory at a 0.8-2% compute-time cost, and requires an invertible activation (leaky ReLU/ELU).
findings.relevance: This is a negative prior for a memory-traffic route via InPlace-ABN. GELU is not invertible, and the published method costs time rather than saving it. Any H2.16 kernel should target fewer HBM passes (fused reductions), not activation-memory reduction.

findings.claim: The benchmark repo (AIDDA-Institute CIFAR-100-speedrun) contains only .gitkeep in submissions/, has 0 PRs and one fork created 2026-10-03. Its verified baseline is a ResNet9 (40 epochs, width 64) at 75.36% mean (range 75.16-75.56) in 59.30 s on the A100 80GB PCIe, judged on 40 trials.
findings.relevance: There are no external competing CIFAR-100 recipes to mine. The loop's ~4.6 s tip is already far beyond any published CIFAR-100 result (futurebiohackers 8.11 s). Further external evidence must come from CIFAR-10 records (Fable, hiverge) and from general literature.

findings.claim: A critical-damping momentum schedule, mu(t) = 1 − 2*sqrt(alpha(t)), reaches 90% on CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 2.34x faster but costs 0.46 pp of final accuracy. The hybrid version recovers it. On CIFAR-100 the early gain shrinks to 1.14x when matched for final accuracy.
findings.relevance: This is weak, long-schedule SGD evidence. It gives no support for a momentum-schedule lever in the ~256-step Muon regime, consistent with the flat Muon momentum results (E030).

findings.claim: Specialist-agent auto-research on airbench96 (CIFAR-10) cut wallclock 4.59% (26.36 -> 25.15 s). 81 of 97 trials missed the accuracy gate. The final speedup came from a shorter horizon, a higher LR intensity and a 'faster warmup' that repaired accuracy after the cuts.
findings.relevance: Generic evidence only. Warmup repair worked there, but the loop's warmup length is closed at 0.23 (E051, E059). It reinforces the H4 lesson that most near-gate trials fail, so pooled baselines are essential.
